name: Softmaxxing

lead: Softmaxxing is the looksmaxxing name for reversible, low-risk improvements such as skincare, haircuts, grooming, clothing, posture, sleep and exercise. It is set against hardmaxxing, which covers surgery and drugs, and forum users commonly advise doing softmaxxes first.

The payoff is cleaner skin, tidier grooming, better body composition and a sharper overall presentation, much of it visible quickly. A looksmax.org guide defines it as non-invasive, reversible, low-risk improvements that raise attractiveness without surgery or medical intervention. The components have their own research, mostly from dermatology and general health guidance, and no trial has tested softmaxxing as a package.

paras: Typical basics include twice-daily cleansing, daily sunscreen, oral hygiene, a flattering haircut, well-fitted clothes, good posture, lifting and weight management. Some people add less conventional practices such as mewing and NoFap, which Grokipedia says have little scientific support.

Most components are low risk. Researchers have noted that online skincare content mixes commercial claims with advice and can encourage irritating self-experimentation, and critics link looksmaxxing culture generally to body-image distress.

angle.text: Softmaxxing covers skincare, haircuts, grooming, clothing, posture and weight management, giving cleaner, healthier-looking presentation with no surgery. Forum guides describe it as low-risk and reversible, and many of the habits show visible results quickly.

lead: Softmaxxing is the looksmaxxing term for non-invasive, reversible ways of improving appearance: skincare, haircuts and grooming, clothing, posture, weight management, sleep and exercise. It is set against hardmaxxing, which covers surgery, off-label drugs and other invasive or extreme methods [1][2]. A looksmax.org guide defines it as non-invasive, reversible, low-risk improvements that raise attractiveness without surgery or medical intervention [3].

How it improves looks is direct and visible: clearer, better-protected skin, a cut and grooming that suit the face, fitted clothes, upright posture and a leaner body that shows the jaw and cheekbones [2][3][2]. Forum guides place it first in the order of operations and commonly advise doing softmaxxes before considering hardmaxxing [3]. Wikipedia notes it overlaps with the grooming advice that men's magazines such as GQ, Esquire and Men's Health have long run [1].

No clinical trials of softmaxxing as a package were found. Research touching the area includes a 2026 narrative review of digital skincare content and acne treatment adherence [4], a 2026 cross-sectional analysis of online discourse on looksmaxxing, softmaxxing and hardmaxxing [5], and dermatology guidance on basic skincare [6][7]. Individual components such as skincare, exercise and sleep have their own, separate evidence bases.
infobox: Skincare, haircut, grooming, clothing, posture, sleep, exercise, weight management [1][2]

paras: Wikipedia describes softmaxxing as simple, non-invasive practices for minor improvements, including skincare, grooming, clothing, weight management and exercise, and says it contrasts with hardmaxxing's extreme practices aimed at larger changes in appearance and facial structure [1]. Looksmax.org guides use a similar definition: reversible, low-risk changes that need no surgery or medical intervention [3].

The boundary is loose. Wikipedia lists less conventional practices such as mewing (a tongue-posture technique) and NoFap (abstaining from masturbation) under softmaxxing, and it classes off-label peptides as hardmaxxing [1]. A forum guide, however, treats peptides as a beginner softmaxx [3], and thread titles apply the word to the nose, personality and mandibular development [8][9].

Wikipedia traces looksmaxxing to message boards of the 2010s, where three forums (PUAHate.com, Sluthate.com and Lookism.net) formed the 'PSL community' and its rating scale; those sites are now defunct but much of the vocabulary survived [1]. The soft/hard split grew up inside this forum culture and later carried over to looksmax.org, which hosts the guides and routine threads cited here [3][10][9].

Looksmaxxing reached TikTok in the early 2020s, where early content was often self-improvement oriented, and by the mid-2020s mainstream coverage tied it more closely to black pill ideology [1]. Wikipedia lists coverage by Vice (2018 and 2023), Business Insider and the New York Times (2023), the Guardian (2024), the BBC (2024), and NPR and Vanity Fair (2026) [1]. Much of the later coverage concerns hardmaxxing and extreme practices, whereas grooming-level softmaxxing content resembles ordinary self-care advice [1].

Skincare is the most common softmaxx. Grokipedia describes basic routines of cleansing, moisturizing and daily sunscreen, sometimes with niacinamide [2][2]. Wikipedia's skin care article says dermatologists generally prioritise gentle cleansing, moisturizing and sun protection, reserve other products for specific conditions such as acne, and note that over-exfoliation can irritate and damage the skin barrier [6]. An expert consensus in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology addresses adoption of holistic routines (cleansing, treatment, moisturization and photoprotection) in acne, rosacea, atopic dermatitis and sensitive skin [7], and a plastic-surgery paper frames daily skincare as having a long-term effect on overall complexion quality [11].

A 2022 paper in Clinics in Dermatology examined 'slugging' as a viral TikTok beauty trend presented as harmless, illustrating how routines spread through social media [12]. The 2026 review of digital acne content describes how clinical advice sits beside commercial claims and transformation stories, and links acne stigma, depressive symptoms and body-dysmorphic symptoms to treatment satisfaction and adherence, while separating associations from proven causes [4].

Grokipedia lists haircuts every few weeks, nose and ear hair trimming, teeth whitening, nail care, tinting of brows, lashes or hair, hygiene and fragrance ('smellmaxxing'), and well-fitted clothing, with fit emphasised over brand [2][2]. In a thread from a 15-year-old asking for tips while cutting weight, replies suggest growing hair out slightly, regular fades, skin care, nutrition and more sleep [10].

Grokipedia describes reducing body fat through a calorie deficit, resistance training and sleep as the biggest single upgrade, because leanness reveals jaw and cheekbone structure, and lists posture cues such as shoulders back and neutral chin [2]. It cites medical guidance recommending gentle twice-daily washing, SPF 30 or higher, oral hygiene, strength training, adequate sleep and avoiding smoking, and states that no formal evidence-based looksmaxxing routine exists [2][2]. Some of Grokipedia's supporting citations are to general consumer pages and clinic sites rather than primary studies [2].

Grokipedia also lists mewing, hard gum chewing and 'thumbpulling' under softmaxxing, naming influencers such as Oscar Patel (thumbpulling routines), Clavicular and Kareem Shami as popularisers, and Zyzz as an early muscular-transformation model, while describing mewing as lacking solid scientific support [2]. Wikipedia describes mewing as an unproven form of oral posture training developed by British orthodontists John Mew and his son Mike Mew within orthotropics; the American Association of Orthodontists says there is no evidence that it improves the jaw, and Mike Mew was removed from the UK dental register in 2024 [13]. Since 2019 it has spread widely on social media, particularly in looksmaxxing circles [13].

Grokipedia cites medical guidance recommending gentle cleansing, sunscreen of SPF 30 or higher and strength training, and says that no formal evidence-based looksmaxxing routine exists [2]. It also states that studies link features such as clear skin, white teeth, stubble or styled hair, fitted clothing and improved posture with higher perceived attractiveness, and gives body-fat and shoulder-to-waist figures from consumer pages; it notes that jawline-sharpening claims from weight loss rest on before-and-after posts, not controlled studies [2].

A 2026 cross-sectional study of social media discourse on dangerous facial aesthetic trends used social-listening, Google Trends and Instagram metrics, followed by a thematic analysis of the 100 most-engaged looksmaxxing posts, and reported that the term bonesmashing produced 2,518 mentions over twelve months with an estimated reach of 32 million, with YouTube the largest source of discourse (43.7 percent) [5]. The paper focuses on hazardous practices rather than on grooming, though it frames softmaxxing and hardmaxxing as the two practice families [5].

No studies found on softmaxxing as a combined practice. Related literature includes a narrative review of digital skincare content and acne treatment adherence [4], a social-listening analysis of looksmaxxing discourse [5], and dermatology literature on routine skincare components [7][11]; none tests whether softmaxxing as a package improves rated attractiveness.

Forum guides frame softmaxxing as the starting point of the looksmaxxing path. One claims that it accounts for 50 to 70 percent of a person's looks potential, a figure given without cited research [3]. Its author describes sleeping long hours, hydration and other basics as foundational, and argues that people who skip them for 'dangerous maxxes' have misjudged priorities [3]. Other threads post 'journey' photos and ask for routine feedback [14][9].

Wikipedia reports critics who describe looksmaxxing culture as linked to body dysmorphia and suicidal ideation, and notes that some men report benefits such as dating success and peer affirmation [1]. Researchers have also described the culture as sitting between self-enhancement and self-harm [1]. Softmaxxing is generally the less contested end of that spectrum, and the 2026 acne review notes that body-dysmorphic symptoms and expectations influence how people experience online skincare content [4].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org softmaxxing is presented as the entry level of looksmaxxing, and guides, 'journey' threads and tip requests are written for newcomers [3][10][14].
